plain_english: Here's a problem we need to answer: both good and bad people experience pleasure. Bad people enjoy their shameful acts just as much as good people enjoy doing noble things. This is why the ancient philosophers told us to live the highest life, not the most pleasant one. Pleasure shouldn't be our guide — it should just come along for the ride when we think rightly and act with honor. Nature should be our guide instead. Let reason keep watch over nature and take its advice. Living happily, then, means living according to nature. Let me explain what this means.
original_excerpt: What answer are we to make to the reflexion that pleasure belongs to good and bad men alike, and that bad men take as much delight in their shame as good men in noble things? This was why the ancients bade us lead the highest, not the most pleasant life, in order that pleasure might not be the guide but the companion of a right-thinking and honourable mind; for it is Nature whom we ought to make our guide: let our reason watch her, and be advised by her. To live happily, then, is the same thing as to live according to Nature: what this may be, I will explain.

plain_english: If we take care of our bodies and natural gifts without being afraid to lose them — remembering they won't last forever and are only on loan to us — if we don't let them control us or become slaves to things that aren't really part of who we are; if we treat all physical pleasures and external rewards like support troops in an army rather than the main force; if we make them serve us instead of the other way around — only then do they actually help our minds. A person should stay independent and not be conquered by outside things. You should admire yourself alone, trust your own spirit, and live your life ready for whatever comes — good luck or bad.
original_excerpt: If we guard the endowments of the body and the advantages of nature with care and fearlessness, as things soon to depart and given to us only for a day; if we do not fall under their dominion, nor allow ourselves to become the slaves of what is no part of our own being; if we assign to all bodily pleasures and external delights the same position which is held by auxiliaries and light-armed troops in a camp; if we make them our servants, not our masters—then and then only are they of value to our minds. A man should be unbiassed and not to be conquered by external things: he ought to admire himself alone, to feel confidence in his own spirit, and so to order his life as to be ready alike for good or for bad fortune.

plain_english: Don't let his confidence be empty — it needs real knowledge. And don't let his knowledge be shaky — it needs firm conviction. Once he decides something, he should stick with it. His beliefs shouldn't be constantly changing. You'll see (even though I don't need to spell this out) that this kind of person will be calm and steady. He'll be noble in spirit and kind in his actions. Let reason work with the senses to find truth. Let it build its foundation there. Reason has nowhere else to start from when hunting for truth. It has to circle back to itself.
original_excerpt: Let not his confidence be without knowledge, nor his knowledge without steadfastness: let him always abide by what he has once determined, and let there be no erasure in his doctrines. It will be understood, even though I append it not, that such a man will be tranquil and composed in his demeanour, high-minded and courteous in his actions. Let reason be encouraged by the senses to seek for the truth, and draw its first principles from thence: indeed it has no other base of operations or place from which to start in pursuit of truth: it must fall back upon itself.

plain_english: Even the universe itself — and God who guides it — reaches out into all external things, yet always returns completely back to itself. Our mind should do the same thing. When our mind follows our bodily senses and sends itself out into the external world through them, it should still remain master of both those senses and itself. This way we will gain a strength and ability that work together as allies. From this we get the kind of reasoning that never wavers between two opinions, and never grows dull in forming perceptions, beliefs, or convictions.
original_excerpt: Even the all-embracing universe and God who is its guide extends himself forth into outward things, and yet altogether returns from all sides back to himself. Let our mind do the same thing: when, following its bodily senses it has by means of them sent itself forth into the things of the outward world, let it remain still their master and its own. By this means we shall obtain a strength and an ability which are united and allied together, and shall derive from it that reason which never halts between two opinions, nor is dull in forming its perceptions, beliefs, or convictions.

plain_english: When your mind gets organized and all its parts work together in harmony, you've reached the highest good. Nothing evil or risky remains. Nothing can shake you or trip you up. You'll do everything according to your own will. Nothing unexpected will catch you off guard. Whatever you do will turn out well — easily and naturally, without needing tricks or schemes. Slow, hesitant action shows your mind is divided and uncertain. So you can boldly say the highest good is unity of mind. Where there's agreement and harmony, the virtues must be present. It's the vices that fight against each other.
original_excerpt: Such a mind, when it has ranged itself in order, made its various parts agree together, and, if I may so express myself, harmonized them, has attained to the highest good: for it has nothing evil or hazardous remaining, nothing to shake it or make it stumble: it will do everything under the guidance of its own will, and nothing unexpected will befal it, but whatever may be done by it will turn out well, and that, too, readily and easily, without the doer having recourse to any underhand devices: for slow and hesitating action are the signs of discord and want of settled purpose. You may, then, boldly declare that the highest good is singleness of mind: for where agreement and unity are, there must the virtues be: it is the vices that are at war one with another.
